title: Highest-Protein Seeds: Ranking Per 100 Grams

seo.title: Highest-Protein Seeds Ranked per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Compare hemp, pumpkin, sunflower, flax, sesame and chia seeds by protein per 100 grams and per realistic one-ounce serving.
seo.search_intent: Rank edible seeds by protein content.

excerpt: Hulled hemp and pumpkin seeds top the list at about 30–32 grams of protein per 100 grams. A realistic ounce contributes roughly 5–9 grams depending on the seed.
content_html:
Seeds are extraordinarily protein-dense by weight, but they are also fat-rich and usually eaten in small portions. Ranking them by 100 grams is useful for concentration; ranking an ounce is better for real life.

SeedProtein/100 gProtein/1 oz
Hulled hemp31–32 gabout 9 g
Pumpkinabout 30 g8–9 g
Sunflower20–21 gabout 6 g
Flaxabout 18 gabout 5 g
Sesame17–18 gabout 5 g
Chia16–17 g4–5 g

Hemp and pumpkin seeds

Both can add close to 9 grams of protein in an ounce. Hemp also supplies polyunsaturated fats; pumpkin seeds contribute substantial magnesium, zinc and other minerals.

Flax and chia have different strengths

Neither leads the protein ranking, but both supply alpha-linolenic acid (ALA). Chia is exceptionally high in fiber. Ground flax generally makes nutrients inside the seed more accessible.

Why serving size matters

Seeds often contain 500–600 calories per 100 grams because they store oil. That is normal seed biology, not a defect. It simply means tablespoons and ounces are more realistic than 100-gram bowls.

What one ounce actually gives you

An ounce is a more useful comparison than 100 g for most meals. Hulled hemp provides about 9 g of protein per ounce, pumpkin seeds roughly 8–9 g, sunflower seeds about 6 g, flax and sesame around 5 g, and chia roughly 4–5 g. That is enough to change the protein content of a bowl of oatmeal or yogurt, but it is still smaller than a full serving of tofu, beans, fish or poultry.

Protein per calorie changes the picture

Seeds commonly provide around 140–170 calories per ounce because they contain substantial oil. Hemp and pumpkin seeds therefore deliver a useful amount of protein, but they are not equivalent to a very lean protein source. The same calories from cooked chicken breast, egg whites or a lean white fish can provide considerably more protein.

This is not a criticism of seeds. Their fat includes unsaturated fatty acids, and they also provide fiber and minerals. It simply explains why a tablespoon of seeds works best as an addition to a meal rather than as the entire protein base.

Hemp versus pumpkin seeds

These two are close enough that the choice does not need to be made on protein alone. Hemp is around 31–32 g of protein per 100 g, while pumpkin seeds are around 30 g. In a one-ounce serving, the difference is roughly a gram or less.

Hemp contributes polyunsaturated fats, while pumpkin seeds stand out for magnesium, zinc and iron. Rotating them gives more variety than treating one as nutritionally superior.

Chia and flax: lower protein, different strengths

Chia provides roughly 16–17 g of protein per 100 g, well below hemp and pumpkin, but its fiber content is exceptionally high. Flax is around 18 g and is notable for ALA omega-3. These differences show why a protein ranking should not be used as a general nutrition score.

Ground flax is usually easier to incorporate into food and makes the nutrients inside the seed more accessible. Chia absorbs water and forms a gel, which changes texture and can make a small serving feel substantial.

Roasted, salted and flavored seeds

Roasting can shift the per-100-g numbers slightly by changing moisture, but it does not remove the protein. Added salt can raise sodium dramatically, while sugar, chocolate coatings or added oils can change calories and the overall nutrient profile much more than roasting itself.

Bottom line

If protein is the only metric, hulled hemp and pumpkin seeds are the clear leaders among common seeds at around 30–32 g per 100 g. In realistic servings they contribute about 8–9 g per ounce. Sunflower, flax, sesame and chia add smaller amounts while bringing different combinations of fiber, minerals and fats.

Frequently asked questions

Which seed is highest in protein?

Hulled hemp and pumpkin seeds are around 30–32 g per 100 g.

Is chia high in protein?

Yes, though at about 16–17 g per 100 g it trails hemp and pumpkin and is more notable for fiber and ALA.

Can seeds be the main protein?

They can contribute meaningfully, but their small portions make beans, tofu, tempeh, dairy or meat more practical main proteins for many meals.

faq.question: Which seeds have the most protein?
faq.answer: Hulled hemp and pumpkin seeds lead common options at roughly 30–32 g per 100 g.

faq.question: How much protein is in one ounce?
faq.answer: Roughly 4–9 g depending on the seed.

faq.question: Are chia seeds the highest-protein seed?
faq.answer: No. Hemp and pumpkin seeds contain considerably more protein by weight.
